html:
The Hồng Đức Code was the law code of Vietnam's Later Lê dynasty, issued under Emperor Lê Thánh Tông in the Hồng Đức era, around 1483. It stayed in force, with additions, until the early 1800s.

It followed the shape of Chinese codes such as the Tang Code and the Great Ming Code, with their scale of punishments and their Confucian ideas of family and rank. Lê Thánh Tông, who ruled Đại Việt from 1460 to 1497, wanted an orderly Confucian state run by examined officials.

But it also kept Vietnamese customs, and is best known for the rights it gave women. Daughters could inherit family property along with sons, and a wife's own property remained hers. A woman whose husband abandoned her for a set time could leave the marriage. These rules gave Vietnamese women more legal standing than women had under Chinese law of the same time, or under the later Gia Long Code of 1815, which followed the Qing model more closely.
